draft.title: Social and economic conditions
card: In 1900 most people in the Russian Empire were peasants who worked the land. Most were poor and had little land of their own.

Serfdom ended in 1861, but peasants still paid redemption payments, a long-term debt for the land they received. Land was often in short supply, and farming methods were old-fashioned, so harvests were low and famine was a risk.
From the 1890s the government pushed fast industrial growth, building railways and factories in cities such as St Petersburg and Moscow. Peasants moved to the cities to find work.

City workers lived in crowded housing and worked long hours for low pay in poor conditions. They had no legal trade unions, and strikes were banned. Many workers stayed close to their villages, and anger over land and conditions grew in both places.
draft.remember: Poor peasants and crowded, badly paid workers both had reasons to be angry.

a.q: Why were many Russian peasants poor around 1900?
opts: They had little land, old farming methods and debts
They were banned from growing food for sale
They had all moved to the cities to work in factories
They paid no debts but were forced into the army
a.why: Peasants often had too little land, used old methods and still paid redemption payments, so harvests and incomes stayed low. Moving to cities is wrong because most people still lived on the land.
a.clue: Think about land, farming methods and debts after 1861.

b.q: Anya moves from her village to a St Petersburg factory in 1905. Which conditions is she most likely to face?
opts: Crowded housing, long hours and low pay
Spacious housing and pay set by a trade union
Her own farm and the end of her debts
Short hours and the legal right to strike
b.why: Fast industrial growth packed workers into crowded housing with long hours and low pay. The other options describe rights or land that most workers did not have, since unions and strikes were banned.
b.clue: Recall what life was like for factory workers in the growing cities.

a.best: They had little land, old farming methods and debts

b.best: Crowded housing, long hours and low pay

problems.detail: The clue ('Think about land, farming methods and debts after 1861') lists the three parts of the right option, so it gives the answer away.
Too easy for Year 12. Distractors such as 'They had all moved to the cities' and 'They paid no debts' are plainly absurd, so a student can pick the answer without knowing the idea.
Too easy for Year 12. Every distractor describes plainly good conditions, so the only negative option stands out without any knowledge.

'They had no legal trade unions, and strikes were banned' is stated with no time frame. Trade unions were legalised, with restrictions, in March 1906. The statement holds before 1906 but is not true for the whole 1890s–1914 period the card spans.

Setting the scenario in 1905, the year of the mass strikes of the 1905 Revolution (point 3), clashes with the claim that strikes were banned. A year such as 1900 would avoid confusion with the next point.

proposal.title: Social and economic conditions
card: In 1900 most people in the Russian Empire were peasants who worked the land. Most were poor and had little land of their own.

Serfdom ended in 1861, but peasants still made redemption payments, a long-term debt for the land they received. Land was short and farming methods were old-fashioned, so harvests were low and famine was a risk.

From the 1890s the government pushed fast industrial growth, building railways and factories in cities such as St Petersburg and Moscow. Peasants moved to the cities for work, and many kept close ties to their villages.
City workers lived in crowded housing and worked long hours for low pay. Until 1906 trade unions were illegal and strikes were banned, so anger over pay and conditions had no legal outlet.
proposal.remember: Land-hungry, indebted peasants and crowded, badly paid workers both had reasons for anger.

a.q: Why did many Russian peasants stay poor after serfdom ended in 1861?
opts: They paid redemption debts on too little land
Landlords still legally owned them as serfs
Factory work had drawn most of them off the land
They farmed huge plots with too few workers
a.why: Freed peasants still owed redemption payments, and land was short while farming methods were old, so harvests stayed low. Saying landlords still owned them is tempting, but serfdom had legally ended in 1861. The problem was debt and land shortage, not serfdom itself.
a.clue: Freedom in 1861 came with a cost attached.

b.q: Anya leaves her village to work in a St Petersburg factory in 1900. Which best describes her situation?
opts: Long hours and low pay, with no legal trade union
Long hours and low pay, but a legal trade union
Crowded housing, but the legal right to strike
Short hours and good housing, but very low pay
b.why: Factory workers faced crowded housing, long hours and low pay, and before 1906 unions were illegal and strikes were banned. The option with a legal union is tempting because it gets the hours and pay right, but in 1900 unions were not yet legal.
b.clue: Check what the law allowed workers before 1906.

a.best: They paid redemption debts on too little land

b.best: Long hours and low pay, with no legal trade union
